cards.b: Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A pair of electrons shared between two atoms, giving each a noble gas electronic configuration.

cards.f: How do metal atoms form ions?
cards.b: They lose outer-shell electrons to form positive ions (cations). Group I forms 1+, Group II 2+.

cards.f: How do non-metal atoms form ions?
cards.b: They gain electrons to complete the outer shell, forming negative ions (anions). Group VII forms 1−, Group VI 2−.
Giant lattice: a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions.

cards.f: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.b: Many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions must be overcome, which needs lots of energy.

cards.f: When do ionic compounds conduct electricity?
cards.b: When molten or in aqueous solution (ions are free to move); not as solids (ions fixed in the lattice).

cards.f: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?
cards.b: Weak intermolecular forces between molecules are easily overcome; covalent bonds within molecules do not break.

cards.f: Why can simple molecular compounds not conduct electricity?
cards.b: They have no ions or free electrons; molecules are uncharged.
Each carbon bonded to 4 others in a giant covalent lattice; very hard, so used in cutting tools.
Layers of carbon, each bonded to 3 others, with weak forces between layers and delocalised electrons. Soft, slippery, conducts.
Each carbon has one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layers.
Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions in a lattice and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together.

cards.f: Dot-and-cross: how many shared pairs in N₂ and O₂?
cards.b: N₂ has a triple bond (3 pairs); O₂ has a double bond (2 pairs).

short.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point. [2]
short.model: It has a giant lattice with strong electrostatic attractions between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, which need a lot of energy to overcome.
points: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions

short.q: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does. [2]
short.model: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
points: molten: ions free to move and carry current

short.q: Explain why methane has a low boiling point. [2]
short.model: It is a simple molecule with weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome; covalent bonds do not break.
points: little energy needed to overcome them

short.q: Explain why graphite is a good lubricant and a good electrode material. [3]
short.model: Layers slide easily because forces between layers are weak; delocalised electrons carry current along the layers.

short.q: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity. [2]
short.model: Metals contain a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move through the lattice and carry charge.
